b.bio: Cesare Baronio, printed here as Caesar Baronius, was born at Sora in the Kingdom of Naples and died in Rome. He joined Philip Neri's Oratory in Rome in 1557, succeeded Neri as its superior in 1593, was made cardinal by Clement VIII in 1596 (cardinal priest of Santi Nereo ed Achilleo), and served as Vatican librarian from 1597 until his death. His Annales Ecclesiastici, twelve folio volumes published between 1588 and 1607, were written as a Catholic reply to the Magdeburg Centuries and narrate church history down to the year 1198. He was declared venerable in 1745 by Benedict XIV.
b.s: The Annales Ecclesiastici here — twelve volumes plus two minor pieces — form the principal Roman Catholic counter-history to Protestant church historiography, defending episcopal succession and papal legitimacy against Arians, Donatists, Photius, Nestorius, Iconoclasts, and Eusebius's account.

b.bio: The library prints one work under 'Ch. Arnoldus': a dedicatory letter preserved in Migne's Patrologia Latina volume 19. None of the better-known medieval authors named Arnold covered by surviving records matches it. Arnoldus Leodiensis (c. 1276–c. 1309) wrote the Alphabetum narrationum for preachers; Arnold of Saint Emmeram (died after 1035) wrote on St Emmeram; Arnold of Brescia (c. 1090–1155) left no surviving writings at all. The letter held here discusses Porphyrius's exile for a false crime, dates poems before the death of Crispus, argues that imitating Porphyrius's artificial verse harms young poets, and disputes points against Jerome and Bede while citing Eusebius, Julian, Fulgentius, Philoxenus, and Plato.
b.s: The single work under this name is a learned dedicatory letter on Porphyrius and poetic imitation, notable chiefly for taking positions against Jerome and Bede.

b.bio: Christoph Brouwer (Browerius) was a Jesuit priest and ecclesiastical historian, born on 12 March 1559 at Arnhem in the Netherlands. He entered the Society of Jesus in 1580, taught philosophy at Trier, and served as rector first at Fulda and then at Trier. At the request of the archbishops Johann VII of Schönenberg and Lothar of Metternich he wrote the Antiquitates et annales Trevirenses et episcoporum Treverensis ecclesiae suffragorum, an annalistic history of the archdiocese of Trier to the year 1600, intended to counter Hermann Kyriander's pro-city account of 1576. He died at Trier in 1617 before completing it.
b.s: The work held here is his prefatory address to the reader for his edition of Rabanus Maurus printed in PL 112; Brouwer matters chiefly as the historian of the archdiocese of Trier whose annals were later published in altered form after his death.

b.bio: Bulgaranus, a count and prefect of Narbonensian Gaul, appears in the record around 612. The two pages of letters held here are addressed in the conflict between King Chlothar II's circle and Brunhild and her grandson Theuderic, arguing that prayer and litanies should precede recourse to arms, that God defends Catholics against perfidious enemies, and that lawful territorial grants must be honored to preserve concord. He cites King Rechared of holy memory. Note: the jurist Bulgarus of Bologna (d. 1166) is a different man sharing a similar name; his career is irrelevant to these letters.
b.s: His letters are a rare lay voice in the Brunhild–Theuderic controversy, framing resistance to the Frankish regime as defense of Catholic unity and legitimate grants.

b.bio: Constantino Cajetan (Gaetani), born at Syracuse, Sicily, in 1560, died at Rome on 17 September 1650. He became a Benedictine at San Nicolò d'Arena in Catania on 29 October 1586, and was soon called to Rome by Clement VIII to edit the works of St. Peter Damian. His research in Roman archives won him Cardinal Baronius's friendship and support for Baronius's Annales Ecclesiastici; he served as custodian of the Vatican Library under four popes and founded the Gregorian College of St. Benedict in Rome, established by Gregory XV's bull of 18 May 1621.
b.s: The works held here are his prefatory letters, dedications, and admonitions to readers attached to his editions — chiefly his four-folio edition of Peter Damian (PL 144–145) and a volume of Benedictine history (PL 163) — which frame the texts with arguments about papal authority, Benedictine contributions to Christendom, and reform of church morals as the pontiff's charge.

b.bio: Guy of Burgundy, son of Count William I of Burgundy, was named Archbishop of Vienne in 1088 and served as papal legate in France under Paschal II. He led the opposition in France to the Privilegium of 1111 by which Paschal yielded to Emperor Henry V, attended the Lateran Synod of 1112, and was elected pope at Cluny on 1 February 1119. His pontificate ended the Investiture Controversy through the Concordat of Worms (1122), and he convened the First Lateran Council in March 1123. Prompted by attacks on Jews, he issued the bull Sicut Judaeis forbidding Christians on pain of excommunication from forcing Jews to convert or harming them.
b.s: The works held here are his letters and privileges — chiefly decretals asserting that violation or contempt of papal privilege incurs excommunication, that interdicts spare infant baptism and deathbed penance, that legitimate petitions must not be delayed, and defending freedom to receive sacraments from any catholic bishop — together with the Concordat of Worms itself, the settlement of the Investiture Controversy with Henry V.

b.bio: Candidus is known only as the Arian author of a treatise on divine generation addressed to the rhetor Marius Victorinus (Epistola ad Marium Victorinum rhetorem de generatione divina), together with a short epistle to him preserved by Mabillon. McClintock and Strong place his activity about 364; Biblissima gives uncertain dates of 350?-372? and records the possibility that the name was invented by Victorinus himself as a foil in his anti-Arian polemic. The works held here argue against Alexander of Alexandria and other defenders of generation from substance, asserting that God is unbegotten from no pre-existing substance and reading Proverbs 8:22 and John 1:3-4 as testimony that Christ was made.
b.s: His two letters are among the few surviving Arian statements on divine generation, preserved because Victorinus answered them at length.

b.bio: An anonymous continuator of Cosmas of Prague's Chronica Boemorum, probably a canon of the Vyšehrad chapter founded by Vratislaus II around 1070 (though he may have been a canon of Prague). He wrote annals covering 1125/1126 to 1141, the reign of Duke Soběslav I, writing contemporaneously down to about 1130, resuming around 1140, as an eyewitness or from eyewitness reports. A partisan of Soběslav, he polemicizes against the duke's enemies — Miroslav, Bořivoj's faction, and others he treats as usurpers and conspirators. He had a mediocre education but a marked interest in astronomical and meteorological signs. An entry on the civil war of 1142 and a miracle of Saint Ludmila was added in 1151/1152 by a hand at St George's, Prague.
b.s: His continuation is the primary narrative for Soběslav I's reign and the first Czech historical text to name the Czech nation as the 'family of Saint Wenceslaus'.

b.bio: The name 'Canutus rex' in this shelf denotes a king whose laws, diplomas, and letter stand in PL 151 — legislative and diplomatic texts citing 'King Cnut,' the laws of the English, Kent, and Edmund of the West Saxons. The surviving records describe other men of similar name (St. Knud IV of Denmark, d. 1086; Robert Canutus of Cricklade, fl. 1170) and do not apply to these works.
b.s: The held works assert the supremacy of the king's peace over church peace and prescribe capital penalties and compensation scales for its violation.

b.bio: Cappidus Stauriensis is named after his birthplace, Stavoren in Friesland, where sources place him as a priest around the year 920. He is credited with lives of saints Lebuin, Otger, Plechelm, and Odulph, and genealogies of the princes of Friesland; these manuscripts were said to have perished in a fire that destroyed the library of Stavoren. Some older writers praised him beyond his merits; others called him a writer of fables or doubted he existed at all.
b.s: The work held here, the Life of Saint Odulph, survives in Migne's Patrologia Latina and shows the hagiographic method attributed to him: preaching and doctrine converting the savage Frisians, miracles confirming the faith of believers, true prophecy attested by fulfillment of prediction, and renunciation of all things for Christ.

b.bio: This entry covers a collective author: the twenty-three cardinals who remained faithful to Alexander III after the disputed election of 1159, when a minority backed Octavian (the 'Ferentine bishop', antipope Victor IV), whom Emperor Frederick Barbarossa supported. The library holds their encyclical letters and their joint letter to Frederick himself. In these texts they defend the canonicity of Alexander's election, argue that the apostolic see must not lack a pastor, declare consecrations by expelled bishops invalid, threaten contumacious schismatics with excommunication, and assert that even a persecuting emperor may be cut off and that the liberty of the church must not be violated.
b.s: Their letters are primary evidence for how loyal churchmen framed papal authority, excommunication of rulers, and resistance to imperial interference during the Alexander III schism.

b.bio: The name as the library prints it, Cardinalis de Aragonia, stands over two papal biographies in Migne's Patrologia Latina: a life of Adrian IV and a longer life of Alexander III. The sources here do not give dates or offices for this author, so none are asserted. A separate Johannes de Aragonia, cardinal from 1456 to 1485 (Giovanni d'Aragona, prince of Naples), appears in CERL and Deutsche Biographie; he belongs to a different century and wrote an oration to Sixtus IV, not these lives, and is not the author of the works held here.
b.s: His two lives narrate the pontificates of Adrian IV and Alexander III and defend the roman see's claims against Emperor Frederick Barbarossa: that lawful papal election cannot be overturned by imperial favor, that secular princes may not judge ecclesiastical causes, and that persecutors of the church may be excommunicated.

w: Copy of a Tradition, or Testament

b.bio: Carilef (Latin Calevisus, French Calais; d. 541) was a hermit from Aquitaine who settled as a solitary on the river Anille in the diocese of Le Mans; the abbey there later took his name (Saint-Calais), though the sources indicate it may have been built in his honor rather than founded by him personally. According to the two ninth-century lives, the only written evidence for his career, he trained as a monk at Ménat or at Micy (sources differ) and was ordained by Maximin of Micy, bishop of Orléans (d. 520). The Vita Carileffi says King Childebert I granted him lands after encountering him while hunting. His successor Laumer continued the house; Siviard, another successor, wrote the Vita.
b.s: The single page held here is a copy of a tradition/testament securing the monastery's property and subjection to episcopal authority in perpetuity — a rare Merovingian charter-type text invoking King Childebert, Innocent, and Turibius.

w: Chapters at the Palace of Ver
Chapters in the Broilo of Compiègne

b.bio: Carloman, eldest son of Charles Martel, succeeded to his father's position in Austrasia in 741 and ruled alongside his brother Pepin the Short. He took the lead in the Frankish church reform carried out with St. Boniface, summoning councils in 742 and 743, establishing bishoprics at Würzburg, Erfurt, and Eichstätt, and securing metropolitan dignity for Boniface. In 747 he withdrew from power, entrusted his lands and children to Pepin, and became a monk first on Mt. Soracte and then at Monte Cassino. He died at Vienne in 754 and was buried at Monte Cassino.
b.s: The works held here are his capitularies — chapters issued at the palace of Ver and in the broilo of Compiègne — which order royal authority to the worship of God and peace, attach public penance to secular penalties for plunder, and regulate oaths of purgation by vassal status; they are primary evidence for how Carolingian rulers legislated on sin, penance, and public order.

b.bio:
Carlomannus (c. 866–884) — Wikisource's Scriptor:Carlomannus gives dates 866 to 6 or 12 December 884 and lists three works: Capitula apud Vernis palatium, Capitula in broilo Compendii, and the Promissio apud Carisiacum held here. He must not be confused with two other Frankish namesakes found in the sources: Carloman of Bavaria (c. 830 – 22 March 880), king of Bavaria and Italy, eldest son of Louis the German; and Blessed Carloman, son of Charles Martel, who renounced secular power in 747, became a monk of Monte Cassino, and died in 756.

Ludovicus II Germaniae (c. c. 804–876) — Ludovicus II Germaniae is Louis the German, grandson of Charlemagne and third son of Louis the Pious, who received the East Frankish kingdom by the Treaty of Verdun in 843 and ruled until his death at Frankfurt in 876. The works held here are his capitularies and diplomas — royal chapters on church discipline, oaths, marriage within forbidden degrees, clerical conduct, and the emperor's duty to enforce correction when admonition fails. Note: the Wikisource headers for these texts label them 'saeculo X', while the biographical sources identify the author as the ninth-century king.
b.s: The library holds his Promissio apud Carisiacum (Promise at Quierzy), a royal undertaking in which the king pledges defense and justice to every bishop and church, while bishops owe him counsel and aid in return — a Carolingian statement of mutual obligation between throne and episcopate.

w: Chapters on the Bishopric of Tongeren

b.bio: Surviving records do not clearly identify this author: they cover Carolus Scribani (1561–1629), Charles de la Rue (1643–1725), Carolus Gallus (1530–1616), and Carolus de Tilly (1642–1698) — different persons of similar names, whose careers do not match a Latin-Fathers shelf or a polemic against Archbishop Hermann of Cologne, and they must not be used for this author. The library holds one two-page work under this name in PL 138, 'Chapters on the Bishopric of Tongeren', which cites Gregory, Nicaea, and the sacred canons, and argues against Hilduin, Henry, and Archbishop Hermann of Cologne.
b.s: The held work is a brief polemic on episcopal office: it defends the canonically elected candidate for Tongeren, denies legitimacy to consecration performed under coercion, treats spoliation of church goods as sacrilege and homicide against God and mother church rather than ordinary theft, holds that ambitious self-promotion to office must be repelled, and reads adversity as medicinal grace rather than damnation.

b.bio: Castor of Apt was a bishop of Apt in Gaul, born at Nîmes about the middle of the fourth century and educated at Arles; he first worked as a lawyer before entering religious life. He founded the monastery of Saint-Faustin at Manauque in Provence, which followed the rule of John Cassian; he initially refused the abbacy but accepted it as successor to the dying first abbot, and was subsequently made bishop of Apt. The sources give differing death dates: September 419 (Smith's Dictionary), c. 420, or c. 423 (Wikipedia). The letter held here is his request to Cassian for an account of Egyptian and Palestinian monastic custom.
b.s: His single extant letter to John Cassian prompted the De institutis coenobiorum (Institutiones Coenobiorum), dedicated to Castor, the work that carried Egyptian and Palestinian monastic practice into the Latin West; the text here praises Cassian as expert in Egyptian monastic doctrine and warns that gifts are distributed variously and presumption without discretion leads to ruin.

b.t: Latin (Anglo-Saxon, active at the Frankish court)
b.bio: Cathwulf (Latin Cathuulfus) was an Anglo-Saxon learned man active in Francia, known only from a single letter to Charlemagne written around 775. His name and letter show an education in the British Isles; he was probably a churchman, though scholars divide over whether monk or priest. He wrote as the king's subject and 'servant' (servulus), addressing him familiarly as 'my Charles', which has led some to suggest a prior role as royal tutor. The letter refers to events from Charlemagne's accession in 768 through the fall of Pavia in June 774, and to nothing later.
b.s: His letter is one of the earliest statements of Carolingian political theology: the king rules as God's minister over a Christian people, with eight virtues marking the just ruler and royal injustice bringing famine, pestilence, and defeat.

b.bio: Catwallon (Catuuallon), son of Duke Conan I of Brittany, was elected abbot of Saint-Sauveur de Redon in 1019/1021 and held the office until 1040. A notice of 22 March 1026 records his late brother Duke Geoffroi I donating the island of Guédel to the abbey. He is credited with fostering monastic foundations in Brittany. The two letters printed under his name in PL 141 are dated by Migne's sources to 1038.
b.s: The works held here are two short letters — one addressed to Hildegard, duke of the Angevins — treating prayer and intercession by sinners (the record asserts both that sinners may intercede for others and that sinners are unfit to do so), God's propitiation through others' prayers, true religion witnessed by works, earthly goods as from God's munificence, prayer to the indivisible Trinity obtaining remission of sins, the eucharistic sacrifice's aid to the faithful's prayers, and the abbot's duty to keep the monastic rule.

b.bio: The library's Celsus is not the second-century Greek philosopher who wrote 'The True Word' against Christianity (fl. c. AD 175–180), nor the first-century Roman medical writer Aulus Cornelius Celsus; those are homonyms and are set aside here. The author held under this name is a Christian Latin writer whose surviving piece, printed in Migne's Patrologia Latina volume 6, is a short preface directed against Jewish unbelief. It cites Isaiah, Paul, Malachi, David, Simeon, and one Jason, a Hebrew Christian, and argues that prophecy left unbelievers without excuse.
b.s: The single work held here is a brief anti-Jewish polemic arguing that reconciliation with God comes only through faith in Christ and that Old Testament prophecy—culminating in God's own witness—publicly manifested Christ at his birth, leaving Israel without excuse.

b.bio: Cencio Savelli, born in Rome around 1150, was a canon at Santa Maria Maggiore before serving as papal chamberlain from 1188, Vice-Chancellor, Cardinal-Deacon of Santa Lucia in Silice (1193), then Cardinal-Priest of Santi Giovanni e Paolo under Innocent III. From 1197 he tutored the future emperor Frederick II. Elected by compromise at Perugia on 18 July 1216, he took the name Honorius III, promoted the Fifth Crusade, approved the Dominican and Franciscan orders, and died in Rome on 18 March 1227. The works held here are liturgical: a Roman Order governing papal ceremony and a short text on Amen.
b.s: The library's two works show him as a legislator of papal ritual — penitential-season vestments, barefoot processions, rank-ordered offerings at papal mass, and vigil orders for city solemnities — not as the crusade-promoting pope his biographies emphasize.

w: For the Catholic Easter and the Roman tonsure

b.bio: Ceolfrith (also Ceolfrid), born in Northumbria in 642 to a family of the highest Anglo-Saxon nobility, became a monk at Ripon under Wilfrid, was ordained priest by him, served as prior of Wearmouth and succeeded Benedict Biscop as abbot of the twin monasteries of Wearmouth and Jarrow. With Benedict Biscop he assembled the fine library available to Bede. He composed the prefatory epigram to the Codex Amiatinus pandect Bible dedicated to St Peter's, Rome. He died on 29 September 716 at Langres on the frontier of Burgundy.
b.s: The work held here is his letter defending the Roman Easter computus and tonsure: it argues that observance of Easter must follow the Roman church, that the scriptural rule for Easter cannot be changed by human authority, that the paschal feast begins on the fifteenth moon (not the fourteenth), that the Lord's day for Easter was added by apostolic institution, and that the paschal full moon must follow the vernal equinox — directed against adherents of the eighty-four-year cycle and Adamnan's Columbians.

b.bio:
Ceretius (fl. 441–450) — Ceretius was a fifth-century Gallic bishop who signed the canons of the Council of Orange in 441 and, in the summer of 450, wrote jointly with Salonius and Veranus to Pope Leo I. Their letter, preserved among Leo's correspondence as epistula 68, thanks him for sending his letter to Flavian and asks him to correct a copy they had made for circulation to other bishops; one such copy reached the bishops of upper Italy through Ceretius' mediation (Leo, epist. 97, 2). A separate tradition identifies him as bishop of Grenoble and gives 450 as his death year.

Salonius of Vienne (c. c. 400–475) — The library prints him as Salonius of Vienne, but the sources identify him as Salonius of Geneva: a fifth-century bishop, son of Eucherius of Lyon and Galla, educated at Lérins Abbey — first under Hilary of Arles, then Salvian and Vincent of Lérins (an older source names Honorat instead of Salvian). In 440 he was elected bishop of Geneva and took part in the Synod of Orange (441), the Synod of Vaison (442), and the Synod of Arles (451); an older source says he is 'supposed' to have assisted at Orange with his father. He died 28 September 475 (one older source says about 470). The works held here are his mystical expositions on Proverbs and Ecclesiastes and a letter to Pope Leo.

Veranus (d. c. 480) — Veranus was the fourth Bishop of Vence in Gaul, son of Eucherius of Lyon and brother of Salonius. Educated at Lérins Abbey under Hilary of Arles, Salvianus, and Vincent of Lérins, he became bishop around 442 and served at least until 465. In February 464 Pope Hilarius commissioned him to warn Mamertus of Vienne against irregular ordinations, upholding the primatial privileges of Arles as defined by Pope Leo I. His father's Liber formularum spiritalis intelligentiae is addressed to him. He should not be confused with the later Veranus of Cavaillon (d. c. 590), a different bishop.
b.s: The work held here is the joint letter to Pope Leo concerning the Tome to Flavian, a document of the reception of Leo's Christology in Gaul.

b.bio: Nothing in The surviving records gives dates or offices for this Chaussier, author of two pieces in PL 95 concerning the antiquity of the church of Metz. The library record shows an apologist for the Metz catalogues: he argues that Christianity reached Gaul in the first century through disciples of the apostles, that Peter sent preachers to the western provinces, and that the church of Metz was founded by such disciples — reopening questions settled by eighteenth-century criticism.
b.s: His dissertation and catalogue are a late defense of the apostolic-origin claims of the church of Metz against Dom Calmet, Dom Cajot, and eighteenth-century critical scholarship.

b.bio: No surviving record identifies this author. The two biographical entries found describe different men with similar names — Jean Jacques Caton Chenevière, a Swiss Protestant theologian born 1783 who taught at Geneva (source:1), and Gentian Hervetus, a French Catholic controversialist of Olivet/Reims (sources:2,4) — and neither can be attached to 'Chenevet'; their biographies must not be used for this author. What can be said comes from the library record alone: a single short historical treatise in PL 185 on the village of Fontaines, treating the chapel there, its patron Ambrosinien, the translation of Aleth's body from St-Bénigne to Clairvaux, and the identification of Bernard of Clairvaux's birthplace tower.
b.s: His work here is a brief antiquarian history of Fontaines arguing that the sanctuary stands in Bernard of Clairvaux's birthplace tower and that the octagon is a late embellishment, not original.

b.bio: Childebert II was the son of Sigebert I and Brunhilda, recognized as king of Austrasia in 575 at about age five after his father's assassination, with his mother dominant during his minority until he came of age around 585. He was adopted as heir by his uncle Guntram of Burgundy and succeeded him there in 592, ruling both kingdoms until his death in March 596. The works held under his name are not theological treatises but royal acts: precepts and a constitution granting villas to bishops and monasteries in perpetuity, asserting that such grants do not violate canon law, that monasteries are immune from secular judges and fiscal exaction, and that monks owe prayer for their royal benefactors.
b.s: The texts here show a Merovingian king legislating for the church — protecting monastic liberty and endowing bishops — and are read as evidence of early Frankish church-state relations rather than as doctrinal writing.

b.bio: Christopher was a Roman, son of a man named Leo, and cardinal-priest of the title of St. Damasus. In October 903 he deposed Pope Leo V and took possession of the papal see; in January 904 he was driven out by supporters of Sergius, who became Pope Sergius III. Though long listed as a legitimate pope in medieval catalogues and acknowledged as such by successors like Leo IX, his uncanonical seizure of office led to his removal from the Annuario Pontificio; he is now counted an antipope. Accounts of his end differ: Auxilius of Naples (per Eugenius Vulgarius) suggests he was strangled in prison alongside Leo V, while Hermann von Reichenau says he was forced to become a monk.
b.s: His single extant act is the diploma confirming the privileges of the Abbey of Corbie — the document held here — asserting papal headship over all churches, the abbey's right to elect its own abbot, freedom from secular judges, and excommunication for resisters of papal privilege.

b.bio: The Deutsche Biographie index dates Chrodebertus Turonensis to about 653/674 and lists him as a bishop of Tours ('Chrodebertus, Episcopus', 'Chrodebert, de Tours'). McClintock and Strong identify Chrodebert I as archbishop of Tours, otherwise called Rigobert or Zerobert, and note that the Chronicon Turonense makes him the prelate who granted privileges to St Martin's Abbey at Tours later confirmed by Pope Adeodatus (672–676).
b.s: The library holds one work under his name, the Judgment concerning the adulterous woman (PL 87); its contents are not further characterized in the library record.

b.bio: Chuonradus II is Conrad II, first emperor of the Salian dynasty: king of Germany from 1024 and emperor from 1027 until his death at Utrecht in June 1039. The library's two works under his name are not theological treatises but royal charters preserved in Migne's Patrologia Latina volume 151: diplomas issued in 1025 and a set of constitutions dated 1031. Their content is legal and ecclesiastical-administrative — grants of immunity protecting church lands from secular judges, confirmation of monastic and conventual elections, tithe arrangements, and dues owed to bishops by written agreement. They argue against Lombard judges and against a prelate of Mainz on points of jurisdiction.
b.s: The works held here are imperial diplomas and constitutions documenting how a Salian king regulated church property, tithes, and monastic elections in the early eleventh century.

b.bio: Cixila was Archbishop of Toledo from about 774 until his death in 783, serving under Muslim rule in most of Spain. A short biography embedded in one manuscript of the Mozarabic Chronicle of 754 (Paris, Arsenal 982) says he had been attached to the church of Toledo since the Arab invasion and had served God from infancy; it has been supposed that he may have known or studied under Toledo scholars such as Urban and Evantius, whom he later names as witnesses for the miracles he records in his Life of St. Ildefonsus. He succeeded Archbishop Concordius and was succeeded by Elipandus.
b.s: His Life of St. Ildefonsus is the main witness to the cult of Toledo's great seventh-century bishop, presenting Ildefonsus's holiness as a heavenly gift whose teaching endures after his death.

b.bio: Suidger von Morsleben-Horneburg, bishop of Bamberg and former chaplain to Henry III, was elected pope on 25 December 1046 after the Council of Sutri deposed Benedict IX and Sylvester III and accepted Gregory VI's resignation. He crowned Henry III emperor and convoked a Roman council in 1047 issuing decrees against simony. He died 9 October 1047 near Pesaro and was buried at Bamberg.
b.s: The letters held here are privileges for monasteries — including Fulda's precedence among German monasteries and abbatial consecration reserved to the apostolic see — documents of the early German reform papacy's assertion of papal authority over monasteries and against simoniacal bishops.

b.bio: Paolo Scolari, born in Rome in 1130, was named cardinal-deacon of Santi Sergio e Bacco by Alexander III in 1179, cardinal-priest of Santa Pudenziana in 1180, and cardinal-bishop of Palestrina from 1181 until his election as pope on 19 December 1187. He ended the six-year exile of the papacy from Rome by treaty with the Roman Commune, created thirty-one cardinals, called the Western princes to the Third Crusade after the fall of Jerusalem in October 1187, released the Scottish Church from York's jurisdiction in 1188, and died in Rome on 20 March 1191 (one source gives 29 March). The works held here are his letters and privileges and decrees, not a treatise by another hand.
b.s: The letters and privileges here show papal government at work: protection of church property, privileges enforced by excommunication and divine judgment, disputes with Baldwin of Canterbury and other bishops, and settlement of jurisdictional claims between mother and daughter churches.

w: Foundation of the College of 16 Clementine Clerics

b.bio: Clemens VI, born Pierre Roger at Maumont in Limousin, entered the Benedictine monastery of La Chaise-Dieu as a boy, studied and taught at Paris, and rose through a series of offices: prior of Saint-Baudile at Nîmes, Abbot of Fécamp, Bishop of Arras and Chancellor of France (1328), Archbishop of Sens (1329), Archbishop of Rouen (1330), cardinal (1338). He was elected pope on 7 May 1342, the fourth Avignon pope, and reigned through the first visitation of the Black Death. The work held here is not one of his doctrinal letters but a foundation charter establishing a college of sixteen Clementine clerics, with rules for residence, oversight, and endowment.
b.s: The single work held here is his foundation act for the College of Clementine Clerics, valuable chiefly for what it shows of papal provision for clergy: continuous residence, weekly recorded absences with forfeiture of distributions, common dwelling, and endowments restricted to perpetual rents.

b.bio: This is not an individual but a collective voice: the clergy and people of the church of Mainz, writing in Latin under that corporate name. The library holds one work under it, a two-page letter addressed to Sigefrid, archbishop of Mainz. The letter pleads that consecration binds a bishop to his flock, that he serves Christ better by feeding his sheep than by withdrawing from them, and that the pastoral care of souls is the bishop's supreme duty — an argument aimed at an absent bishop and at the monastic party around him. It appeals to Luke xii, to Peter, Paul, and the other apostles, to the decrees of the church and the canons, and to the apostolic see.
b.s: The letter is evidence of how a cathedral community pressed its archbishop on the duties of office, framing episcopal residence as obedience to Christ's command to feed his sheep.

b.bio: Clovis, son of Childeric, succeeded as king of the Salian Franks at Tournai in 481 and died at Paris on 27 November 511. He defeated Syagrius at Soissons in 486, conquered rival Frankish kingdoms, the Alemanni, and the Visigothic kingdom of Aquitaine, and united the Franks under a single kingship. Baptized between 498 and 506, largely through the influence of his wife Clotilda, he founded the Merovingian dynasty that ruled for over two centuries.
b.s: The single page held here is a royal precept exempting clerics and religious from military plunder and ordering the restoration of captives taken from church persons, showing Clovis governing by reference to the apostolic see.

b.bio: Clovis II, son of Dagobert I and Nanthild, succeeded his father as king of the Franks in Neustria and Burgundy in 639, while still a child, and reigned until his death in 657. Sources give his birth year as 633 or 635; he was buried at Saint-Denis. About 649 he married Balthild, later regarded as a saint, by whom he had three sons who succeeded him. The works held here are not theological treatises but royal diplomas: charters confirming monastic property, granting privileges to bishops such as Landericus of Paris, and endowing perpetual psalmody at Saint-Denis on the model of Agaune.
b.s: His diplomas show how Merovingian kingship exercised itself through grants to churches and monasteries — clemency toward petitioners, inviolable donations to saints' shrines, and royal confirmation securing ecclesiastical property.

b.bio: Chlotar I (printed here as Clotaire I), son of Clovis I, received Soissons and the old Salian lands when the kingdom was divided in 511. He murdered his nephews after Clodomir's death in 524, shared in the conquests of Thuringia and Burgundy, and by outliving his brothers became sole king of the Franks in 558. He died at Compiègne in late 561, and his four surviving sons divided the kingdom again. The single page held under his name is a royal constitution on law, hearings before condemnation, marriage consent, protection of churches and clerics, and thirty years' prescription.
b.s: The work here shows a Merovingian king legislating on church immunity, lawful judicial procedure, and marriage — loci later treated under the civil magistrate and true worship.

w: Edict on the Synod of Paris
Precept for the Monastery of St. Denis

b.bio: Chlotar II (Clotaire II), son of Chilperic I and Fredegund, became king of Neustria as an infant in 584 under his mother's regency and his uncle Guntram's protection. After defeating Brunhilda and her grandsons, he united all Frankish kingdoms under his rule in 613. His reign saw growing power of nobles and church; the Edict of Paris (614) gave legal force to canons of a council held at Paris while modifying them with restrictions, extended ecclesiastical tribunals' competence, and regulated offices and taxation.
b.s: The works here are royal acts — precepts, an edict on the Synod of Paris, and letters — showing a Merovingian king legislating for the church: asylum in church atria (with restitution rules for fugitive slaves), penalties for theft and refusal to pursue thieves, and the binding force of conciliar decrees made in God's name; one text argues against Arnulf.

b.bio: Chlothar III was the eldest son of Clovis II and Balthild; he succeeded his father as king of Neustria and Burgundy in 657 while still a child, under his mother's regency, and briefly ruled Austrasia before Childeric II was sent to be king there in 662. After Balthild retired to a monastery in 664 or 665, real power lay with the mayor of the palace Ebroin. The work printed here under his name is not patristic theology but royal diploma material: charters restoring lands to monasteries, granting immunity from tolls and royal exactions, and binding the king and his successors perpetually, with prayer owed by the monks in return.
b.s: The single work held here preserves Merovingian royal privilege on behalf of monasteries — land restoration, perpetual exemption from tolls, and adjudication against Beracharius — showing how royal gifts to saints were framed as securing eternal reward.

b.bio: Charles Cocquelines was an eighteenth-century Roman editor and publisher of papal documents; his Bullarum privilegiorum ac diplomatum Romanorum Pontificum amplissima collectio (Rome, 1733–), printed at Typis S. Michaelis ad Ripam, gathered papal bulls together with lives of all the popes. He also published Giovanni Pietro Maffei's Degli annali di Gregorio XIII pontefice massimo (1742) and an edition of P. Terentius Afer. He should not be confused with the French poet-theologian Nicolas Cocquelin (1640–1693) or the nineteenth-century economist Charles Coquelin.
b.s: The items held here under his name are the historical notices prefixed to popes' lives in his bull-collection, which Migne's Patrologia reprinted; they narrate a lawfully elected pope restored against a usurper of the see, whom they treat as a schismatic pseudo-pope, arguing against Gregory.

b.bio: Guido di Castello, born in Città di Castello or possibly Macerata, studied under Peter Abélard and became a distinguished master in the schools before beginning his career in Rome as subdeacon and scriptor apostolicus under Callixtus II. Honorius II made him cardinal-deacon of Santa Maria in Via Lata in December 1127; Innocent II later raised him to the cardinal priesthood (c. 1134) and sent him as legate to France (1140), where his protection of Arnold of Brescia incurred Bernard of Clairvaux's displeasure. Elected pope on 26 September 1143 (consecrated 3 October), he at once lifted Innocent's interdict on Louis VII of France over the Bourges election, and died on 8 March 1144 on the eve of a conflict with Roger II of Sicily.
b.s: The single work held here is a collection of his letters and papal privileges defending monasteries — chiefly Stavelot — through grants of free burial (except to excommunicates), inviolability of church possessions confirmed by papal privilege, and excommunication for violators, asserted against Cluniac claims (Abbot Peter of Cluny), the bishops of Gaul, and local harassers of Stavelot.

w: Summary of the Epistle to the Roman Clergy

b.bio: Coelestius, a native of Ireland by general report, studied law in Rome and attached himself to Pelagius about 405. He fled the Gothic advance to Sicily, then to Carthage, where a council under Bishop Aurelius condemned his teaching in 412 for denying original sin and the need of grace. Refused ordination there, he obtained priesthood at Ephesus, appealed to Pope Zosimus in 417, and was condemned with Pelagius at the Council of Ephesus in 431.
b.s: The works held here — on original sin, impeccability, faith addressed to Zosimus, and a summary to the Roman clergy — represent the Pelagian side of the controversy that forced Augustine's doctrine of grace into shape; his writings survive today only in fragments.

b.bio: Caelius Symphosius is known only as the author of the Aenigmata, a collection of one hundred Latin riddles in hexameter tercets, transmitted with their solutions. Even his name appears to be a joking pseudonym. Proposed dates of composition have ranged from the third to the sixth century; the prevailing view places them in the late fourth or early fifth century, and circumstantial evidence in the riddles suggests Roman North Africa. The preface presents them as Saturnalia entertainment, possibly a literary convention, and their form draws on Martial's Xenia.
b.s: The Aenigmata became the model for medieval Latin riddle collections, especially in England, where it provoked a literary vogue and served as a school text; Aldhelm is the earliest ancient witness to it.

b.bio: Cogitosus was an Irish monk, most likely of Kildare, who wrote the oldest extant Life of Saint Brigid. In the epilogue he calls himself 'nepos culpabilis haedo', 'the blameworthy descendant of Áed', compelled by obedience by the community of Kildare to write; whether this means kinship with Brigid is disputed—Ware and Ussher thought him her nephew, while his editor Vossius denied it, and the Catholic Encyclopedia notes his mention of a long succession of bishops and abbesses points to a date after Brigid's death (d. 525). Muirchú moccu Machtheni names him the first Irish hagiographer. The Dictionary of Irish Biography suggests 'Cogitosus' may be a Latinized nom de plume for the rare Irish name Toimtenach.
b.s: His Vita Sanctae Brigidae is the earliest surviving life of St Brigid and a key source for early Irish monasticism, church order, and art; his description of the church of Kildare is specially interesting for the history of early Irish art and architecture.

w: Funeral Poem on the Death of Charlemagne

b.bio: Columbanus of Saint-Trond was a French poet and abbot of the monastery of Saint-Trond (Trudo), said to have died about the middle of the ninth century. A dirge on the death of Charlemagne circulated among the works of Rabanus Maurus under a subscription naming a certain Columbanus, and Muratori identified this Columbanus with the abbot of Saint-Trond; to him is also attributed De Origine atque Primordiis Gentis Francorum, written about 840 and dedicated to Charles the Bald. Modern scholarship treats the attribution of the Charlemagne lament as disputed and probably mistaken, since the poem is generally considered anonymous, likely by a monk of Bobbio shortly after Charlemagne's death in 814.
b.s: The library holds his Funeral Poem on the Death of Charlemagne (PL 106), an early planctus mourning the emperor as protector of orphans, widows, pilgrims and virgins, though its ascription to him is contested; modern scholarship regards the poem as anonymous.

b.bio: A provincial synod of Gallic bishops held at Carpentras on 8 November 527, under the consul Mavortius and Pope Felix IV. Sixteen bishops attended, with Caesarius of Arles presiding. The council issued a single canon regulating parish revenues: offerings given by the faithful to parishes belong to the clergy serving them and to church upkeep; a bishop may claim a surplus only when his own church's resources are insufficient for his expenses. The same act suspends Agroecius, bishop of Antibes, for one year for ordaining contrary to the canons.
b.s: Its one canon is an early witness to the protection of parish property against episcopal exaction, and its suspension of Agroecius shows conciliar discipline over illicit ordination in sixth-century Gaul.

b.bio: The name covers the episcopal councils held at Carthage in the mid-third century while Cyprian was bishop there. The acts printed in Migne's Patrologia Latina vol. 3 belong to the synods that dealt with the lapsed — Christians who had sacrificed or otherwise compromised during persecution — and with the schism that grew out of the question of restoring them. The same gatherings condemned the schismatic party of Felicissimus at Carthage and rejected the legates and letters of Novatian, who in Rome refused reconciliation to any lapsed person. The acts survive only through citations and later collections; Cyprian's letters are the chief witness to what was decided.
b.s: These acts record the African church's settled discipline for the lapsed: penance required before restoration, but peace never finally withheld from the dying penitent — the position that defeated Novatianism.

b.bio: Council of Causey (unknown) — The name as printed ('Council of Causey') does not match any body described in The surviving records, which concern other persons entirely (Caesarius of Arles, Caesarius of Heisterbach, Cyprian); they cannot be used for this author. No dates or composition can be asserted from them. The library record identifies the held work as conciliar acts printed in Migne's PL 139 whose theses concern the deposition of a contumacious bishop, the removal of a 'tyrant bishop' for the good of people and kingdom, coercion of rebel bishops by the prince on the authority of African synods, and opposition to restoring one Arnulf as a revival of tyranny against kings. These are concerns of late tenth-century Frankish episcopal politics, not patristic-era Gaul.
b.s: Per the library record, the acts here defend royal and synodal power to depose bishops, citing Augustine, African councils, and popes Boniface, Zosimus, Leo, and Gregory against the defenders of Arnulf and Roman tyranny under Crescentius.

b.bio: The Council of Chalcedon was summoned by Emperors Valentinian III and Marcian to settle the Christological controversy. The acts name Celestine of Rome and Cyril of Alexandria among the authorities invoked, and cite Rusticus the deacon behind the Latin translation tradition of the acts. The council reaffirmed the Creed of Nicaea as the right and immaculate faith and the Constantinopolitan definition as confirming the same apostolic faith, declared that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father and is worshipped, affirmed one baptism for the remission of sins, and confessed one Christ in two natures against both Nestorius and Eutyches. Its Definition states that the Nicene creed suffices for knowledge of piety.
b.s: Its Definition of Faith is a classical Chalcedonian statement confessing one Christ in two natures, opposed to Nestorius and Eutyches.

b.bio: The Council of Clermont was a mixed synod of clerics and laymen summoned by Pope Urban II and held from 17 to 27 November 1095 at Clermont in Auvergne, attended by roughly 300 French clerics. Its main business was the implementation of Cluniac reform: renewal of the Truce of God, extension of the excommunication of Philip I of France over his marriage to Bertrade of Montfort, decrees against lay investiture by princes, rules forbidding clerical arms-bearing and restricting episcopal eligibility to deacons or priests, and penalties against simoniacal purchase of benefices. On 27 November Urban preached the call to arms that launched the First Crusade, responding to appeals relayed via envoys of the Byzantine emperor Alexius I Comnenus; Fulcher of Chartres, present at the council, gives the account generally accepted as the most reliable.
b.s: The canons printed here are the council's reform legislation — peace-of-God provisions granting perpetual peace immunity to clerics, monks and women, truce-day protections, penitential crusading vows that satisfy all penance, discipline against lay investiture, clerical arms-bearing, and simoniacal purchase of benefices — issued alongside the sermon that began the First Crusade.

b.bio: This entry covers the assembly of eastern bishops convened at Constantinople in 381 by Theodosius I, meeting in the church of Hagia Irene from May to July. It confirmed and expanded the Creed of Nicaea into what became the Niceno-Constantinopolitan Creed, and was recognized as ecumenical only later, at Chalcedon in 451. The library holds its synodal letter to the western bishops, which reports the council's proceedings and asks for their approval: it recounts the deposition of heretical bishops, defends the ordinations made at Constantinople, cites Nicaea's 318 fathers, the Council of Aquileia, and the Synod of Antioch, and confesses one substance in three hypostases against Sabellians, Arians, Eunomians, Pneumatomachi, and Apollinarians.
b.s: Its letter is a primary witness to how the council understood itself — a regional synod seeking western ratification — before later tradition ranked it the second ecumenical council.

b.bio: Concilium Hispalense is the name under which this library holds two Latin texts printed in Migne: a canon on the reservation of episcopal functions to bishops (PL 55) and a chapter on communities of consecrated virgins (PL 88). The surviving records describe Isidore of Seville (c. 560–4 April 636), archbishop of Seville, who in 619 pronounced an anathema against ecclesiastics who molested monasteries; they do not describe or date these specific texts. Whether the held canons belong to a council at Seville associated with Isidore or another assembly bearing the same name cannot be established from what is given.
b.s: The two works here are disciplinary canons asserting that altar consecration, ordination by imposition of hands, and baptism in the bishop's presence are reserved to bishops, and that monks may govern houses of virgins but keep no familiar intercourse with them.

b.t: Latin Church (Lotharingian) (inferred from the named bishops of Reims, Verdun and Trier)
b.bio: Council of Mouzon (unknown) — The library holds two pages of acts printed under the name Council of Mouzon in PL 139. The record shows a synodal text concerned with excommunication and self-condemnation: no bishop may excommunicate without confession, conviction, or refusal to amend, and no one may condemn himself without consciousness of guilt. The acts cite Gerbert, archbishop of Reims, Aymo of Verdun, Liodulf of Trier, Abbot Leo, and John 15, and argue against positions attributed to a 'John xv' and a 'Leo'. the surviving records describe the Benedictine abbey of Notre-Dame de Mouzon (re-established by Archbishop Adalbero of Reims in 971) and its church, not the council itself.
b.s: The surviving fragment is an early witness to canonical limits on excommunication asserted at a tenth-century Lotharingian synod.

b.bio: A provincial synod held in the cathedral of Ravenna in 997, in the second year of Emperor Otto III's imperial reign, presided over by Gerbert of Aurillac as archbishop of Ravenna. The acts printed in Migne's PL 139 record a series of disciplinary canons: subdeacons are forbidden to sell consecrated hosts or chrism to bishops and archpriests, on pain of anathema; archpriests owe an annual census to the see; bishops may not act in another's diocese without consent; clergy transfers require canonical letters from the Nicene synod; ordination requires age, doctrine, and canonical fitness; and payment for burials by clergy is forbidden.
b.s: The acts here are early evidence of anti-simony legislation in Ottonian Italy.

w: Selections from the Council of Reims

b.bio: Council of Reims is catalogued in the collection under Latin Fathers with the works held recorded as Acts.
b.s: The councils held at Reims between the 7th and 12th centuries were significant regional and papal synods addressing church discipline, simony, investiture, and theological controversies.

b.bio: Council of Reims (fl. 991) — The Council of Reims of 991, usually called the Synod of St-Basle, was convoked at Reims by King Hugh Capet, assisted by Gerbert of Aurillac, to try Arnulf, Archbishop of Reims, illegitimate son of the late King Lothair, for conspiring with his uncle Charles, Duke of Lower Lorraine, against Hugh. The council deposed Arnulf and appointed Gerbert in his place, without papal approval; Pope John XV refused to accept either act. The dispute dragged on until Arnulf's restoration in 995 and final resolution by Pope Gregory V in 997.
b.s: Its acts here defend the deposition of Arnulf on grounds that the church must judge its own or seculars will coerce it, that one bishop's crime disgraces the whole episcopal order, and that holy councils require free and orderly procedure — key texts in the medieval contest between royal, episcopal, and papal jurisdiction.

b.bio: The library holds two works under this name, and they are not from the same assembly. One set of acts (PL 3) concerns the dispute over rebaptism of heretics and argues against Cyprian and the African church; its record asserts that rebaptism of heretics caused schism. The other (PL 139) is a set of acts arguing against Conon, bishop of Perugia, the abbot of Perugia, and the bishops of Perugia, and also against Sylvester II and the Roman church's position; it cites John, Gregory, Augustine, Vincentius Lirinensis, Stephanus, Cyprian, and Eusebius. No surviving record here gives dates for either assembly.
b.s: These acta matter as evidence of how Roman councils defined sacramental practice (rebaptism) and disciplined bishops, preserving the Roman side of the rebaptism controversy with Cyprian and the African church.

b.bio: A provincial council held at Rouen, presided over by John, archbishop of Rouen, whose name the acts cite. The canons printed in PL 147 legislate on sacramental and disciplinary matters: chrism consecrated by a bishop with twelve priests, communion obligatory for the celebrant of mass, fasting and vestments required for baptism, confirmation given with fasting and fire, ordination confined to Sunday after the Sabbath fast. The council also condemns named abuses: archdeacons' detestable customs, reservation or reconsecration of hosts beyond the eighth day, and buyers and sellers of parish churches.
b.s: The acts here are a compact witness to Norman liturgical discipline and episcopal control of parish churches, citing Leo and the four ecumenical councils as authority.

b.bio: A synod held at Tours in 1060, part of the eleventh-century reform movement against simony and clerical marriage. The sources also record a Merovingian Council of Tours of 567 (edited by Maassen, MGH Conc. 1, and de Clercq, CCSL 148A), a different body with different acts; the library's text is not that one. The 1060 acts are printed in Migne, Patrologia Latina 143.
b.s: The two pages held here are canons of the 1060 reforming council: they declare simoniacal ordination void for giver and receiver, reserve ecclesiastical office to clerics, require celibacy on pain of deposition, strip benefices from clergy who bear arms, regulate lay possession of churches (requiring episcopal consent), require restoration of alienated church property, bind conciliar decrees by authority of the Holy Spirit, and allow appeal of irregular ordination to the apostolic see. The text cites the Council of Chalcedon and a Pope Nicholas — an early witness to the program later associated with Gregory VII.

b.bio:
Council held at Seligenstadt (fl. 1023–1026) — A general council of twelve bishops of the Mainz province, summoned by Archbishop Aribo of Mainz and meeting at Seligenstadt, first in 1023 and again in September 1026. The 1023 session issued disciplinary canons on fasting, marriage seasons, priestly conduct at mass, and lay behavior; canons 16 and 18 touched the contested Hammerstein marriage, whose appeal to Rome led Benedict VIII to withdraw Aribo's faculties. The 1026 session deferred judgment in the Gandersheim jurisdictional dispute between Mainz and Bishop Godehard of Hildesheim to a future royal hearing.

Burchard of Worms (c. c. 950–1025) — Burchard was born after the middle of the tenth century to a noble family in Hesse, educated at Coblenz and elsewhere, and entered the service of Archbishop Willigis of Mainz, who ordained him deacon, made him first chamberlain, and primate or judge of the city. In 1000 Emperor Otto III appointed him bishop of Worms; Willigis consecrated him at Heiligenstadt. He rebuilt Worms's walls and, with Henry II's approval, destroyed the stronghold of Duke Otto that sheltered criminals. Between 1023 and 1025 he promulgated the Leges et Statuta familiae S. Petri Wormatiensis for impartial justice. He died 20 August 1025.
b.s: The acts here are provincial disciplinary legislation of the early eleventh-century German church, drawing on books of canon law and earlier synods such as Mainz 950; they show episcopal regulation of worship, sacramental discipline, and marriage before the Gregorian reform.

b.bio: Conon of Praeneste (Cuno/Kuno von Urach), a German of the family of the counts of Urach (son of Count Egino I) and a canon regular who was among the founders of Arrouaise around 1090, was created cardinal-bishop of Palestrina by Paschal II in 1108. As legate he held synods in France and Germany, excommunicated Emperor Henry V repeatedly over lay investiture, spent six years pressing the acceptance of Thurstan of York as archbishop without subjecting York to Canterbury, and refused consideration for the papacy in 1119.
b.s: The letters held here are instruments of Gregorian ecclesiology: they defend contested episcopal elections by appeal to apostolic authority, argue that election follows the sounder part rather than the majority, compel reluctant electees to accept office, and assert that bishops may excommunicate kings—here deployed against the count of Nevers, the canons of Milly, and Theogerus, bishop-elect of Metz.

w: Preface to Frederick III, Elector of Saxony

b.bio: Conrad Celtes (born Konrad Bickel or Pickel) was a German humanist born at Wipfeld in Lower Franconia on 1 February 1459; he died at Vienna on 4 February 1508. He studied at Cologne (B.A. 1479) and Heidelberg (M.A. 1485), where Dalberg and Agricola taught him, then lectured as a travelling scholar at Erfurt, Rostock, and Leipzig. Frederick III crowned him poet laureate at Nuremberg in 1487, the first German so honored, and he later taught poetry at Ingolstadt and Vienna.
b.s: The work held here is Celtes' preface dedicating his edition of a recovered ancient text to Frederick III, Elector of Saxony, defending the editing of old manuscripts against detractors.

w: On the Passion of Blessed Emmeram the Martyr

b.bio: Constans sacerdos is a Frankish priest of the eighth century whose only surviving work is the Tractatus de passione Beati Emmerammi martyris, printed in PL 96. Wikidata identifies him as Constans Emmerammensis, active in the 8th century; no dates of birth or death are recorded. The treatise narrates the martyrdom of Emmeram and argues that the cause, not the punishment, makes the martyr: Emmeram's cause exceeds those of all other martyrs.
b.s: His tract is an early witness to the cult of St. Emmeram and to early medieval theories of martyrdom, holding that desire for martyrdom flows from love of Christ and that saints bear others' sins in imitation of Christ's passion.

w: On Common Places Necessary for a Physician to Know

b.bio: Constantine the African (Constantinus Africanus) was a physician from Ifriqiya, born around 1015–1020 — the Catholic Encyclopedia says at Carthage, Britannica says Carthage or Sicily — whose native language was Arabic and who also knew Greek and Latin. After travels in Egypt, Syria, India, Ethiopia, and Persia he arrived in Italy at Salerno, then became a Benedictine monk at the abbey of Monte Cassino (joined 1077), where he spent his last decades translating Arabic medical works into Latin. Sources disagree on his death date: Britannica and the Catholic Encyclopedia give c. 1087; Wikipedia says he died before 1098/99.
b.s: He initiated the translation of Arabic medical works into Latin, a development that profoundly influenced Western medical learning. The work held here argues that medicine is a true science and the end of all philosophy, taught only from experimentally proven knowledge, against acute men who deny medicine is a science, citing Hippocrates and Galen.

b.bio: Flavius Valerius Constantinus, Roman emperor and son of Constantius Chlorus. He made the persecution of Christians illegal by signing the Edict of Milan in 313, funded church-building, commissioned new copies of the Bible, and summoned councils of theologians, most notably Nicaea (325). The works held under this name are imperial letters, edicts, decrees and sermons preserved in the Patrologia Latina: they restore confiscated church property, grant liberty of religion to all men, order Easter kept on one common day, and assert the Son's consubstantiality with the Father. The mined citations are overwhelmingly self-references by the emperor ('Emperor Constantine Augustus'), as expected in rescripts issued in his own name.
b.s: The first Christian Roman emperor: these letters and edicts are primary documents of the legal establishment of Christianity and of imperial intervention in doctrine, including against Arius and the Meletians.

b.bio: The library's name points to the bishop of Albi whom McClintock and Strong list as attending the Council of Rheims in A.D. 625 (source:1). Other men named Constantius appear in the same cyclopedia entry — a priest of Lyons and friend of Sidonius Apollinaris, a bishop of Uzes, a correspondent of Avitus of Vienne — but these are distinct figures of the fifth century and are not this author. The sources give no dates for the bishop of Albi beyond his appearance at that council.
b.s: He is held here only as the author of an epistle printed in Migne's Patrologia Latina volume 87; the record gives no further description of its contents.

b.bio: An anonymous writer known only as the continuator of a work begun by one 'Laurentius'. No surviving record gives his name, dates, or office, so none can be asserted. The eight pages held here are a Latin historical narrative centered on Abbot Cono: his restoration and adornment of his monastery, his acquisition of altars for the church, the pope's honor paid him above all prelates, and the many worthy disciples he formed. The account is framed polemically against Emperor Frederick II and the citizens and jurors of Verdun, treating contention between kingdom and priesthood as a cause of schism and reading divine judgment upon seditious usurpers.
b.s: The single short text here is a thirteenth-century monastic history and polemic preserving the cult and cause of Abbot Cono amid the papal-imperial conflict over Verdun.

w: Encyclical Letter on the Death of Suger

b.bio:
Council of Saint-Denis (fl. mid-12th century) — The author here is the corporate voice of the abbey or council of Saint-Denis near Paris, writing in the twelfth century. Its single work held in this library is an encyclical letter announcing and mourning the death of Abbot Suger of Saint-Denis.

William (unknown) — The library prints this author only as William, and no surviving record identifies him. The three Williams in the sources — William Durandus (d. 1296), William of Canterbury (fl. 1170s), and William of Saint-Thierry (d. 1148) — belong to different centuries and careers, and none is documented as writing this letter; they are treated here as namesakes, not as the author. What can be said comes from the work itself: an encyclical letter announcing the death of Abbot Suger, addressed to King Louis and Pope Eugenius III, indicating composition among French ecclesiastical circles of the mid-twelfth century.
b.s: The letter is a contemporary collective obituary for Suger: it frames his death as a happy exchange rather than a loss, urges moderated grief between despair and ingratitude, asserts that a virtuous life guarantees a glorious death, that death is common to nature while grace is singular, and that the faithful dead join the number of the elect.

w: Sermon on the Life of St. Zeno

b.bio: A Veronese notary named Coronatus wrote the Sermo de vita Zenonis, a short account of the life of Zeno of Verona. His floruit is variously placed in the 7th century (Wikipedia) and the 8th century (Wikisource); either way he is known almost solely through this work. In it he reports that Zeno was a native of Mauretania who taught children in Africa and later followed Athanasius of Alexandria to Verona around 340. A different Coronatus, a poet of the Latin Anthology recorded by Smith's Dictionary and the Perseus catalog, is a separate figure and is not this author.
b.s: His sermon is an early source for the life of Zeno of Verona; the held text credits Christ with omnipotence over demons, shows miracles converting gentiles to faith, affirms that invocation of saints with faith grants petitions, and that saints intercede for the sick at their tombs.

b.bio: Cosmas Japygus is known only through a single poem, the Carmen in honorem sanctorum Theopompei et sociorum, printed in Migne's Patrologia Latina 133. Ughelli's preface reports that the work was read in an old parchment codex of the abbey of Nonantola, which kept the feast of Theopompus and his companions on 4 January. Documenta Catholica Omnia dates him to c. 950 and styles him 'Materiensis'; Wikisource assigns the poem to the ninth century. Nothing else about his life or office is recorded in these sources.
b.s: His surviving work is a verse passion celebrating the martyrs Theopompus and companions, who are said to have suffered at Nicomedia under Diocletian — though Baronius doubted that chronology — and it asserts their intercession for the faithful.

b.bio: Cosmas of Prague, born about 1045 in Prague to a knightly family, studied grammar and dialectics at Liège under Franco, acquiring the classical learning evident throughout his writing. He entered ecclesiastical life at Prague while still young, was ordained deacon in 1094 and priest on 11 June 1099 at Gran (Esztergom) in Hungary. Earlier, while a minor cleric, he had married Božetěcha; their son Henry (Zdík) became Bishop of Olomouc. He joined the cathedral chapter of St. Vitus and became its dean, enjoying close ties with the bishops of Prague and the confidence of Bohemia's rulers.
b.s: His Chronica Boemorum is the first history of Bohemia and the foundational text of Czech historiography; the library holds an excerpt from it in PL 166 treating providence, true worship against pagan sacrilege, the diffusion of peoples after Babel, and the Přemyslid origins of the duchy.

b.bio: Cuthbert (unknown) — This is Cuthbert, the author of the Life of Bede printed in PL 90, not the better-known Cuthbert, bishop of Lindisfarne (d. 687), whose life Bede himself wrote; all supplied web sources describe that other saint and are set aside as concerning a different person of the same name. In his Life of Bede, Cuthbert records Bede's birth around 677 in Northumbria near Jarrow, his entry into the monastery aged seven under Benedict Biscop, and the unity of Wearmouth and Jarrow as one house in two places; he frames his account of Bede's death as commendation rather than argument.
b.s: His Life of Bede is a witness to details of Bede's career at Wearmouth–Jarrow and to his death, corroborated (per the work itself) by Durham tradition and English chroniclers from Simeon of Durham to Capgrave; the work appears to be a later continuation rather than a contemporary eyewitness account.

w: Oration on the Day of His Passion

b.bio: The library prints this name as 'Cyprian of Antioch', and the two short orations held here — on the day of his passion and for the martyrs — are not by Cyprian of Carthage (c. 210–258), whose life the attached sources describe. They belong to the body of pseudo-Cyprianic pieces printed in Migne's PL 4 alongside the genuine works of the bishop of Carthage. Their author is unidentified; no source gives dates, birthplace, or office for him. A separate legendary martyr named Cyprian of Antioch exists in hagiography, but nothing connects these prayers to him either.
b.s: These two orations show how prayer, penance, and confidence in Christ's intercession were voiced in early Latin devotional prose under Cyprian's name.

b.bio: The library's single item under this name is a hymn for St. Benedict printed in Migne's Patrologia Latina 89, a medieval Latin composition praising Benedict's merits, his power over poison through the sign of the cross, and help granted through his prayer. No surviving record here concerns this author: the Cyprian sources describe Cyprian of Carthage (c. 210–258), bishop and martyr — a different person of a different century — and must not be used for this note. No source gives dates or offices for the author of this hymn.
b.s: The hymn attests medieval devotion to St. Benedict, crediting healing and protection to his intercession.

b.bio: Cyprian of Córdoba was an Andalusi Christian poet writing in Latin, active around 890. He served as archpriest in the diocese of Córdoba and moved among the city's leading Christian families: several poems name local aristocrats, and one praises Count Adulfo, who commissioned work from him. His dated poem is an epitaph for Samson of Córdoba, who died on 21 August 890; another commemorates a local martyr named John. Seven (or eight) short poems survive as the Epigrammata, preserved only in the tenth-century Azagra codex (Biblioteca Nacional de España no. 10029). They were written as memorial or dedicatory verses to be placed at the front or back of Bible copies.
b.s: His Epigrams are rare surviving Latin verse from ninth-century Córdoba, and their themes—prayer for the author's salvation, prayers benefiting the departed dead, contemptus mundi rewarded in heaven—show the devotional concerns of Andalusi Christianity.

b.bio: Quiricus (printed here as Cyricius) was bishop of Barcelona from about 653–654 until his death around 666, in the Visigothic period. He attended the Tenth Council of Toledo in 656 and corresponded with Ildefonsus of Toledo and Taio of Zaragoza. Three letters survive: two to Ildefonsus — one thanking him for his treatise on the perpetual virginity of Mary, the other urging him to expound obscure passages of Scripture — and one to Taio. Some scholars identify him with a later Quiricus, bishop of Toledo (d. 680), but this is uncertain.
b.s: The work held here is his surviving correspondence (three letters, PL 96), valuable chiefly as evidence of the learned circle linking Barcelona, Toledo, and Zaragoza in seventh-century Spain.

w: Dissertation I on the Author, Date, History, and Editions
Dissertation II, on the Origin, Family, and Deeds of Frederick I

b.bio: Karl Georg Dümge was a German historian, archivist, and librarian. The works printed under his name in PL 212 are not patristic texts but his critical dissertations prefacing the medieval poem Ligurinus, which celebrates the deeds of Emperor Frederick I Barbarossa. In them Dümge argues that Gunther's traditional attribution of the poem is unsupported by any medieval witness, that Gunther's name arose from confusion with Solymarius via a Constantinople poem, that the poet names himself as Ligurinus, and that the author was an Italian ecclesiastic but not a monk. He engages at length with Senckenberg, Withof, Scioppius, Rittershusius, and others, citing Otto of Freising and Rahewin.
b.s: His dissertations in PL 212 settle the authorship question of the Ligurinus for readers of that edition, arguing against Guntherine attribution on textual and historical grounds.

w: Argument to Bede's book On the Reckoning of Time

b.bio: The library prints this author as 'The Cologne Editors', a collective attribution under which it holds one item: the prefatory argument to Bede's book On the Reckoning of Time as printed in PL 90. No surviving record identifies any individual or group by that name, so no dates, offices, or careers can be asserted here.
b.s: The single work held here is a prefatory argument to Bede's On the Reckoning of Time, treating Scripture and asserting that corporeal things exist only in place while spiritual things are non-local, and that five nations share one scriptural truth in Britain.

b.bio: The library prints this name over two pieces prefacing the Migne Patrologia Latina volume of Bruno of Segni: a long Prolegomena and a brief notice On St. Bruno. No surviving record identifies this author; the sources given concern other men named Charles Emmanuel or Carlo Emmanuele and cannot be used for him. The Prolegomena argues that Bruno of Segni wrote the disputed homilies, defends his eucharistic doctrine against Berengar, and cites Gregory VII, Urban II, Paschal II, Leo the Great, Pius VI, Victor III, and a Victor Amadeus.
b.s: His Prolegomena is the historical-critical case for attributing the disputed homilies to Bruno of Segni and for reading Bruno as a defender of real presence against Berengar's teaching.

w: On the Antiquity and Authority of the Exordium

b.bio: Crisóstomo Henríquez, printed here as Chrysostomus Henriquez, was born in Madrid in 1594 (one source gives 1595). He entered the Cistercian abbey of Huerta at thirteen and made profession there in 1612. Sent to the Low Countries at the request of his parents through Archduke Albert, he was commissioned by his superiors to write the history of the Cistercian Order, visiting Flemish monasteries such as Aulne, Villers, and the Dunes to collect materials. He died at Louvain on 23 December 1632 (one source gives 23 October) and was buried at La Vignette.
b.s: The works held here are historical monuments of Cistercian monasticism: they present God's singular providential preservation of the monastery, Mary as special protectress of the Cistercians, virtuous prelates as preservers of monastic discipline, and saints as exemplary witnesses for the church, citing Bernard of Clairvaux heavily.

b.bio: Ida, countess of Boulogne (c. 1046–1113), mother of Godfrey of Bouillon. She founded the abbey of Wast in the diocese of Boulogne, for which a canon/monk wrote her vita shortly after 1130. The PL 155 materials printed under her name are not writings by her but documents about her: several lives, a letter from Bishop Osmund of Astorga to her (1059), and a genealogy of the counts of Boulogne. The library's single holding, 'Ecclesiastical donations' (PL 155), belongs to this dossier of charters and records connected with her foundations.
b.s: The work held here documents the religious patronage and family of Ida of Boulogne rather than any theological writing by her.

w: Notes on the Code of Canons

b.bio: Christophe Justel, born in Paris in 1580 and died in 1649, was a French Protestant scholar, genealogist and canonist. He served as counsellor and secretary to King Henri IV, purchasing the office for his son Henri Justel, and from 1610 to 1623 was secretary to the Duke of Bouillon. He was charged with forming the public library attached to the Protestant Academy of Sedan. His principal work, the Codex canonum ecclesiae universae (1610–18), collected the ancient Greek and Latin codes of church law; it was reissued in 1661 by Guillaume Voël and Henri Justel as the Bibliotheca juris canonici veteris. He also edited the Nomocanon of Photius with Balsamon's commentary.
b.s: The works held here are his editorial apparatus to the ancient canonical collections — notes, preface, and address to the reader — in which he surveys patristic citations (Zonaras, Epiphanius, Jerome, Cyprian, Tertullian) on ordination, episcopal jurisdiction, clerical celibacy (including the prohibition of subintroduced women), and the limits of Roman claims against Innocent I and Celestine.

b.bio: No source identifies a person named Claude Lepelletier matching these works. The candidates supplied describe other men entirely: Claude Lepelley (1934–2015), a modern historian of Roman North Africa; Louis Le Pelletier (1663–1733), a Benedictine Breton linguist; and Claude Le Laboureur (1601–1675), a Lyon clergyman and genealogist. None wrote the material printed here. The nine pages held under this name are Merovingian-era formularies: model documents for royal grants to churches, confirmation of elected bishops, episcopal elections, and monastic abbatial elections, citing Benedict, Walafrid of Reichenau, Sardica, Nicaea, Chalcedon, and Salic law.
b.s: The work here is not an author's treatise but a collection of ancient formulas—template charters and letters showing how Frankish royal power, episcopal election, and church privilege were legally expressed.

b.bio: The library's record identifies this author only by the printed name 'Ludovicus comes', represented by a two-page response printed in PL 159 among the polemical literature of the Investiture Controversy. the surviving records describe other men of similar Latin names — Ludovicus a S. Carolo, a seventeenth-century Carmelite librarian, and Louis de Blois (Blosius), abbot of Liessies — neither of whom wrote anti-Henrician polemic in PL 159; they are homonyms and are disregarded here. Nothing beyond the printed name and the work itself is established.
b.s: His response is one voice in the Gregorian case against Henry IV, arguing that power commanded against God must be disobeyed, that only ordained power is from God, that simony makes one a heretic, that the excommunicate loses all power over Catholics, and that peace with the wicked is impossible and forbidden — directly answering appeals to Romans 13.

b.bio: Matilda of Tuscany, also known as Countess Matilda of Canossa, was an influential Italian noblewoman and ruler who played a decisive role in the medieval Investiture Controversy. A devoted ally and protector of the reform papacy, she supported Pope Gregory VII and hosted the historic 1077 meeting at Canossa where Holy Roman Emperor Henry IV performed penance. Throughout her rule over extensive territories in northern and central Italy, she provided military and political backing to successive popes and bequeathed vast estates to the Holy See upon her death.
b.s: She was the primary political and military defender of the Gregorian reform papacy against imperial encroachments in northern Italy.

b.bio: Countess Matilda (c. 1046 – 24 July 1115) — Matilda of Canossa, countess of Tuscany and margravine of the House of Canossa, ruled a broad domain across Lombardy, Emilia, Romagna, and Tuscany from about 1055 until her death on 24 July 1115 (the Catholic Encyclopedia gives 1114). She was educated in Latin and was a close ally of the reform papacy; her castle of Canossa was the site of Henry IV's penance before Gregory VII in January 1077. From 1080 she waged near-continuous military conflict against Henry IV in support of papal authority. The volume held here under her name is not her own writing but material associated with her: Donizo of Canossa's Vita Mathildis and her charters and diplomas as printed in Migne's Patrologia Latina 157.
b.s: The works here are the life and diplomas of the laywoman whose patronage and arms sustained the Gregorian reform during the Investiture Controversy.

b.bio: Rémi-Casimir Oudin was born at Mézières-sur-Meuse on 14 February 1638, the son of a weaver. He joined the Premonstratensians in 1655 to devote himself to study, became professor of theology at the abbey of Moreau in 1669 and grand-prior the next year, and later served a church at Épinay-sous-Gamaches in the diocese of Rouen. Confined by his superiors in 1692 after an intimacy with the Protestant controversialist Jurieu, he escaped to Holland and made an open profession of Protestantism, becoming a librarian in Leyden. His major work is the Commentarius de scriptoribus ecclesiae antiquis.
b.s: The works held here are his historical and literary notices and dissertations prefixed to Patrologia Latina volumes — critical judgments on authorship and authenticity (Bede's genuine versus spurious writings distinguished by Bede's own index, the Ephemeris attributed to Germanus of the thirteenth century rather than earlier, the computus on intercalary months not being Bede's, and the nineteen-year cycles belonging to Abbo of Fleury) that shaped how readers identify the Latin Fathers printed in these volumes.

b.bio: The library holds one work under this name, an Admonition printed in Migne's Patrologia Latina vol. 173, but no source consulted identifies its author. The Camillo Pellegrino documented in the sources is a different man entirely: a poet and primicerio of the Cathedral of Capua (c. 1527–1603), member of the Accademia dei Sereni, known for the dialogue Il Carrafa o vero Della epica poesia (1584), which opened the quarrel over Tasso versus Ariosto. He died in 1603 and wrote nothing that would fall in a Patrologia Latina volume of patristic and medieval texts. Nothing can be asserted about the author of the Admonition held here.
b.s: The single work held here, the Admonition of PL 173, cannot be attributed to any documented Camillo Pellegrino on the evidence available.

b.bio: The library holds under this name only a twelve-page preface printed in Migne's Patrologia Latina volume 122. No surviving record identifies the person behind the initials C.B. Schlueterus or gives dates, offices, or places for him.
