The modern writers named Schlueter found in the sources — the contemporary Catholic author Greg Schlueter and the modern biblical scholar Carol J. Schlueter — are different people of different centuries and are not this author.
b.s: His presence here is limited to a prefatory text in PL 122; readers should treat the attribution as that of an otherwise unidentified medieval Latin editor or compiler rather than a documented figure.

w: On the Preeminence and Authority of the Holy See

b.bio:
Claude Sommier (1661–1737) — Jean-Claude Sommier, printed here as Claude Sommier, was born at Vauvillers in the diocese of Besançon on 22 July 1661 and died at Saint-Dié on 5 October 1737. A doctor of theology, he served as preacher to Duke Leopold I of Lorraine, took part in state negotiations, and in 1725 Benedict XIII consecrated him titular Archbishop of Caesarea in Cappadocia and made him grand-prévôt of Saint-Dié. His principal works were the Histoire dogmatique de la religion and the Histoire dogmatique du Saint-Siège (1733), surveys proving religion and papal authority from Scripture and the Fathers.

Cajetan Cenni (unknown) — No source identifies an author 'Cajetan Cenni' as the writer of the work held here. The sources describe two different men with similar names: Gaetano Cenni, an Italian paleographer active at Rome in the early 18th century, author of De Antiquitate Ecclesiae Hispanae (1740–41) and studies of the Codex Carolinus; and Constantino Cajetan (Cajetani), a Sicilian Benedictine born at Syracuse in 1560 who died at Rome on 17 September 1650, appointed by Paul V custos of the Vatican Library, first president of the College de Propaganda Fide, and editor of Peter Damian and Isidore of Seville. Neither biography matches the content of the volume held under this name, which argues against Donatists, Pelagians, Dioscorus, and Novatian while citing Augustine and Cyprian — material from the patristic age, not from either man's lifetime.
b.s: The work held here belongs to his dogmatic-history project: a citation-survey arguing that Peter's successors hold supreme governing power, temporal power by divine providence, and the sole supreme tribunal, marshalling Augustine, Cyprian, Jerome and others against Donatists, Pelagians, Novatian and Dioscorus.

b.bio: Surviving records do not clearly identify this author; they concern a modern South African cardinal (Stephen Brislin), Stephen Langton, Stephen Kim Sou-hwan, and Stephen I Báncsa — different men and centuries, and must not be used here. The works held in PL 143 identify a cardinal named Stephen who acted as a papal legate: he wrote to John of Dol and recorded proceedings at the Council of Bordeaux, where he asserted that a papal legate exercises delegated jurisdiction over bishops, defended the church of Credon's belonging to Vendôme against the monks of Saint-Aubin, and maintained that papal definitions may not be re-judged.
b.s: His letters are evidence for how an eleventh-century papal legate understood delegated jurisdiction over bishops and the finality of papal judgments.

b.bio: Claude Vaussin, born 1608, came from an influential bourgeois family of Dijon and was half-brother of Jean Bouchu, president of the Parlement of Burgundy. He professed at Clairvaux on 1 October 1633, took a doctorate in theology at the Sorbonne, and served as prior of Froidmont before his election as abbot of Cîteaux on 2 January 1643, succeeding Cardinal Richelieu. His election was contested by the Strict Observance; after investigation it was repeated on 10 May 1645, and papal and royal confirmation let him take office in 1649. He governed the order until his death at Dijon on 1 February 1670.
b.s: The work held here is a single epistle printed in PL 210; since the Patrologia Latina closes well before the seventeenth century, this text most likely belongs to a different, earlier writer of the same name rather than to the abbot described in the sources.

b.bio: Charles de Villiers de L'Isle-Adam was a French bishop who held the see of Beauvais and died on 27 September 1535, according to Hierarchia Catholica (via Catholic-Hierarchy). The library holds under his name a single dedicatory letter (PL 141), which argues that goodness of life surpasses learned eloquence, that liberal studies serve virtue rather than outward show, that truth lies in the middle way, and that recovering the fathers confutes heretical slanderers. It cites classical authors (Pliny, Seneca, Claudian, Caesar) alongside Epiphanius and the editor Petavius, suggesting it may have prefaced an edition of patristic texts. Other men named Villiers/Villers in the sources — Pierre de Villiers (1648–1728), Cosme de Villiers (1683–1758), and Charles de Villers (1765–1815) — are different persons and are not this author.
b.s: His surviving work here is a humanist dedicatory letter defending patristic scholarship as an antidote to heretical slander, a window into early-sixteenth-century French editorial culture.

w: Historical Account of the Life and Death of Alan

b.bio: Charles de Wisch (Karel/Carolus de Visch) was born at Bulskamp near Veurne in Flanders on 15 August 1596 and died at Bruges on 11 April 1666. He entered Ten Duinen Abbey in 1618, studied philosophy and then theology at Douai under Francis Sylvius and George Colveneere (Bachelor of Sacred Theology, 1625), served as the abbey's librarian, taught moral theology at Eberbach from October 1630 until Swedish advances in the Thirty Years' War forced his return in late 1631, and was confessor to the Cistercian nuns of Groeninge at Kortrijk before becoming prior of Les Dunes in 1646. His principal work is the Bibliotheca scriptorum S. Ordinis Cisterciensis (Douai 1649; corrected and augmented ed. Cologne 1656). The pages held here are his prefatory matter to the 1654 Douai edition of Alan of Lille's Opera omnia.
b.s: The works here are his historical account and dedicatory apparatus for Alan of Lille's collected works, arguing that Alan was a Belgian born at Lille who presided over the Paris theological school, lived and died as a Cistercian lay brother, and died in 1294 — while disputing claims by Thomas Dempster, Jeremias Drexel, Gaspar Jongelinus, and Angelus Manriquez, and declaring the 1608 Merlin commentaries spurious.

b.bio: Carlos Antonio de la Serna Santander was born at Colindres, Spain, on 1 February 1752 and died in Brussels on 23 November 1813. He entered the Society of Jesus and, after its suppression in 1773, settled in Brussels, where his uncle Dom Simon de Santander introduced him to bibliophilism. He served as librarian of the École centrale de Bruxelles and later as conservator of the Bibliothèque de Bruxelles (from 1795), becoming a specialist in incunabula; he was a corresponding member of the Institut national's history class from 1808. His published work was chiefly bibliographical, written in French.
b.s: The library holds his historical-critical preface to the Spanish canon collection attributed to Isidore of Seville (PL 84), a polemical defense of the collection's genuineness against Voellus, Justellus, Pithaeus, Hincmar of Reims, and others who treated it as interpolated.

b.bio: Carlo Luigi Buronzo del Signore, printed here in Latin as Carolus Burontio del Signore, was born at Vercelli in October 1731 (sources give 22 or 23 October) and died there on 22 October 1806. He took a degree in utroque iure at Turin on 26 June 1751, was ordained priest on 6 October 1754, and received a canonry at Vercelli cathedral on 1 May 1760. An erudite with paleographical interests, he traveled to France, Flanders and Holland in 1764, meeting the Benedictines of St.-Maur in Paris. He was elevated to the see of Aqui in 1784, translated to Novara in 1791 and to the archbishopric of Turin in 1797, then resigned and retired to Vercelli. His chief scholarly work was an edition of the Opera of Atto, tenth-century bishop of Vercelli (Vercelli, 1768), which Migne reprinted in PL 134; the Admonition and Dedication Letter held here belong to that edition.
b.s: The two pieces held under this name are the prefatory matter of his 1768 edition of Atto of Vercelli: a dedication asserting that the prince is guardian of religion and letters, and an admonition arguing that patristic texts must be restored from the autograph.

b.bio: Claude du Molinet, born at Châlons-sur-Marne on 22 July 1620, professed in the Congregation of the canons regular of Sainte-Geneviève in 1641. He administered the abbey library from about 1662 and was librarian in title from 1675 until his death in Paris on 2 September 1687, also serving as procurator general of the congregation in 1676. He built the abbey's cabinet of curiosities, collected Greek and Oriental manuscripts, and was known for numismatic expertise, publishing a history of popes from medals (Martin V to Innocent XI) and an edition of the epistles of Stephen, bishop of Tournai.
b.s: The works held here are his editorial apparatus for Stephen of Tournai in PL 211: a historical notice, an index, and a preface — the scholarship of a seventeenth-century antiquary who made Stephen's letters accessible to later readers.

b.bio: Candidus Isaurus was an Eastern Roman historian, probably born in the 430s, who claimed to be a native of Isauria Tracheia and was a Chalcedonian Christian. He claimed to have served as secretary (hypographeus) to the most powerful among the Isaurians — probably the emperor Zeno and the other Isaurian generals — which suggests he lived in Constantinople for at least part of 474–491. His three-book Greek history covered 457–491, from Leo I's accession to Zeno's death, and was written between Zeno's death in 491 and Anastasius I's purge of the Isaurians in 492. It survives only in fragments: Photius reviewed it and provided a synopsis in his Bibliotheca (cod. 79), and a few Suda passages supplement it.
b.s: The work held here is Photius' synopsis of Candidus' lost history: an orthodox Chalcedonian account of Leo I's and Zeno's reigns, valuable as a near-contemporary witness to events like Aspar's murder, Basiliscus' betrayal of the African fleet, Odoacer's seizure of Italy after Augustulus, and Illus' revolt with Pamprepius proclaiming Leontius emperor against Zeno.

b.bio: Constantine Harmenopoulos was a Byzantine jurist of Armenian descent, born in 1320. He wrote the Procheiros Nomos or Hexabiblos in 1344–45, a six-book compilation of existing Byzantine legislation organized thematically for judges' use, and shortly afterwards was appointed katholikos kritēs, universal judge, of Thessalonica — one of the highest judicial offices in the empire. The Hexabiblos was first printed at Paris in 1540 and formed the basis of Greek civil law under Ottoman rule and in the modern Greek state until the new Civil Code came into force in 1946. Beyond the Hexabiblos he compiled canonical material; his De haeresibus belongs to his wider canonical oeuvre and to the mid-fourteenth-century theological conflicts around Gregory Palamas and hesychasm.
b.s: The work held here is his canonical-heresiological compilation: a citation-survey drawing chiefly on Basil the Great, the Councils of Carthage, Laodicea, and Trullo, treating church order (deacons subordinate to presbyters in order; ordination without metropolitan letters is void), sacraments (heretical baptism requires rebaptism; baptism requires adequate catechetical preparation), and cataloguing heresies from Manichaeans and Bogomils to Massalians and Arians.

w: Manuel Caleca, Monk of the Order of Preachers

b.bio: Manuel Kalekas, a Byzantine theologian and rhetorician born in Constantinople, was a disciple of Demetrios Kydones and an advocate of union with the Western Church. He taught himself Latin to read Thomas Aquinas, translated Boethius and Anselm into Greek, and rendered the Comma Johanneum from the Vulgate. His anti-Palamite writings led to his summons to subscribe to the Tome of Palamas (1351); he refused, was sanctioned, and fled to Pera. He reproached Emperor Manuel II in a letter of 1396, returned with the emperor in 1403, found himself unwelcome, and took refuge with the Dominicans at Mytilene, where he died in 1410. The library's heading calling him 'Patriarch of Constantinople' is an error: there is no evidence Kalekas held that office; it confuses him with John Calecas, Patriarch of Constantinople (1334–47), to whom a family relationship is attested.
b.s: The work held here (PG 152) is his systematic defense of the Filioque and scholastic Trinitarian theology against the Palamites and the Greeks, arguing that the Spirit proceeds from the Father through the Son and that Augustine clearly taught this doctrine.

b.bio: Constantine Lascaris was born in Constantinople in 1434 and educated there under John Argyropoulos. After the fall of the city in 1453 he went to Italy, where Francesco Sforza made him Greek tutor to his daughter Hippolyta; his Erotemata, a Greek grammar written for her and printed at Milan in 1476, was probably the first book printed entirely in Greek. He lectured at Naples in 1465, then settled in Messina on Cardinal Bessarion's recommendation to teach Greek to the Basilian monks, remaining there until his death in 1501. He was chiefly a teacher and copyist of manuscripts; among his pupils was Pietro Bembo.
b.s: A leading Byzantine exile who carried Greek learning into Renaissance Italy, remembered above all for what was probably the first Greek book printed from the press; the library holds a short PG 161 collection whose pages touch on rhetoric, grammar, and moral topics rather than systematic theology.
